nature-nbs-231.title: Scoring how well farms can weather climate change
nature-nbs-231.text: How ready is a country's farming for a hotter, less predictable climate? The Climate-Resilient Agriculture Index tries to put a number on it. The global version benchmarks countries with nine indicators in three dimensions: productivity and resource efficiency, environmental sustainability and climate impact, and socio-economic resilience. It sorts nations into four levels, from Highly Resilient to Very Low Resilience. A version for India uses 26 indicators to compare its agro-climatic zones.

nature-nbs-230.title: Climate-smart farming that works for women
nature-nbs-230.text: Women farmers in developing countries face more climate risk than men. They have less access to land, money and advice. They are also often left out of decisions, which can limit their use of practices that help them adapt. Gender-responsive climate-smart agriculture designs programs around the different constraints and abilities of women and men farmers.

nature-nbs-291.title: Conservation tillage: disturbing the soil less
nature-nbs-291.text: People have stirred the soil mechanically, called tillage, since at least 3000 B.C. Conservation tillage is a group of practices that reduce how much the soil is tilled. No-till and strip tillage are both forms of it, though no-till is not the same thing as the whole group. By 2014 more than 75% of Canadian Prairie cropland had adopted it.

nature-nbs-301.title: Hügelkultur: buried wood that holds water
nature-nbs-301.text: Rotting logs can water a garden. Hügelkultur is burying wood in mounds or beds so it soaks up water and keeps the soil moist. With enough buried wood, the mound can hold rainy-season water and carry crops through the dry season.

nature-nbs-298.title: The three ethics of permaculture
nature-nbs-298.text: Permaculture rests on three core ethics: care of the Earth, care of people, and setting limits to consumption while sharing the surplus. Mollison formulated them in 1988. In 2002 Holmgren restated the third as setting limits to consumption and reproduction and redistributing surplus.

nature-nbs-299.title: Permaculture zones: placing things by how often they are used
nature-nbs-299.text: A permaculture design is laid out in zones numbered 0 to 5, moving outward from the house. Each part is placed by how often people use it. Things tended or harvested often go close to the house, in zones 1 and 2. Things used less go farther out, saving daily walking and effort.

nature-nbs-300.title: Plant guilds: species that help each other
nature-nbs-300.text: A plant guild is a mutually beneficial group of species, each providing a different service within a larger ecosystem. One may supply food. Another may draw up deep nutrients or fix nitrogen. Others attract helpful insects or repel pests.

nature-nbs-303.title: Rainwater harvesting: catching rain before it runs off
nature-nbs-303.text: Rain that runs off a roof is water lost. Rainwater harvesting collects and stores rain for later use before it runs off or soaks into the ground. It supplies drinking water, livestock water and irrigation. Collecting from roofs can significantly add to drinking water supply.

nature-nbs-302.title: Sheet mulching: copying the forest floor
nature-nbs-302.text: A forest floor is a thick blanket of leaves and wood. Sheet mulching copies it by layering leaves, cardboard and wood chips over soil. The mulch absorbs rain, cuts evaporation, adds organic matter, suppresses weeds and reduces erosion. Regenerative farmers also use it to smother weeds and feed the soil.

nature-nbs-256.title: Green manure: a crop grown to feed the soil
nature-nbs-256.text: Some crops are grown only to be plowed back in. Green manure is a cover crop grown to raise soil fertility, usually turned into the soil before it matures. Green manures are commonly legumes, which are high in nitrogen and can supply what the next crop needs. They replace nitrogen that conventional farms apply as chemical fertilizer.

nature-nbs-292.title: Organic farming: natural inputs, fewer synthetics
nature-nbs-292.text: By 2022, 4.5 million farmers in 188 countries were farming about 96,000,000 hectares organically, and the market reached $150 billion. Organic farming relies on natural inputs such as compost, manure and green manure, and on methods like crop rotation. It largely bans synthetic pesticides and fertilizers, and prohibits genetically modified organisms, sewage sludge, growth hormones and routine antibiotics. It began early in the 20th century as a reaction to fast-changing farming. Its environmental record is disputed. On average 30% more species live on organic farms. But a 2012 meta-analysis found organic farming needs 84% more land for the same harvest. Emissions per hectare are lower, yet nitrogen leaching per unit of food is higher. There is not enough evidence that organic food is safer or healthier.

nature-nbs-250.title: Syntropic agroforestry: food forests that follow succession
nature-nbs-250.text: In Brazil, Ernst Götsch developed a way of farming that imitates a forest regrowing. Syntropic agroforestry is an organic system that copies natural forest succession to build productive food forests. It relies on dense mixed plantings of perennial and annual crops. Fast-growing pioneer plants are cut to build up nutrients. Documented benefits include better water penetration, higher productivity on poor land and moderated soil temperature.

nature-nbs-293.title: Organic certification: who gets to say organic
nature-nbs-293.text: Organic certification is the set of rules, voluntary or legal, that define how organic food must be produced and allow it to be labeled organic. Private groups certified organic producers in the 1970s. Legislated standards spread after the 1991 EU regulation, and by 2007 over 60 countries regulated organic farming. Agencies usually accredit certification groups rather than individual farms.

nature-nbs-294.title: The organic price premium
nature-nbs-294.text: In 2013, organic vegetables sold for 100% more than conventional ones, and organic fruit for 57% more. That extra price, the organic premium, is key to whether organic farming pays. With premiums, US organic farming was 2.7 to 3.8 times more profitable, and globally 22–35% more. Only 5-7% was needed to break even. But premiums have narrowed, weakening the incentive to convert.

nature-nbs-295.title: The organic yield gap: can organic feed the world?
nature-nbs-295.text: A 2012 meta-analysis found organic productivity on average 25% lower than conventional. That difference is the organic yield gap, and it drives a debate over whether organic farming could feed the world. The gap depends on crop and site: about 5% for rain-fed legumes and perennials, about 13% under best organic practice. In 2007 the FAO said organic farming could not feed the current population. Estimates vary widely.

nature-nbs-257.title: Trap crops: luring pests away
nature-nbs-257.text: A trap crop is grown to lure pests away from the valuable crop. Once pests gather, the small trap area can be treated or the pests removed by hand or machine. Mustard and radish trap nematodes, tiny soil worms, cutting their populations by 70–99%.

nature-nbs-270.title: Plastic on the farm
nature-nbs-270.text: Farming produces 10 million tons of plastic waste a year, a 2021 FAO study estimated. It comes from greenhouse sheeting, storage bags, silage wrap and mulch film, and much ends up in farmed land. Very little agricultural plastic is collected worldwide.

nature-nbs-272.title: The risks of using living things against pests
nature-nbs-272.text: Releasing predators, parasites or pathogens to fight farm pests can cut pollution from pesticides. But the method carries its own risk. Once released, an agent may be impossible to recall. It may spread into the wild or switch to native hosts. The merits of introducing non-native control agents remain widely debated.

nature-nbs-271.title: How much warming comes from livestock?
nature-nbs-271.text: The FAO estimated that 18% of human greenhouse gases come directly or indirectly from livestock, more than from transport. Critics called the comparison unfair. The FAO counted livestock's whole life cycle but not transport's. Others claim livestock could cause up to 51% of emissions. Estimates remain disputed.

nature-nbs-273.title: Managing manure
nature-nbs-273.text: One dairy farm with 2,500 cows makes as much waste as a city of around 411,000 people, the EPA suggests. Manure management handles and treats animal waste to limit air, soil and water pollution. Treatment reduces the manure to transport, the nutrients to spread and the pathogens. Anaerobic digestion breaks down liquid manure without air, yielding fertilizer liquid and methane to burn for heat and power.

nature-nbs-269.title: Pesticides that linger for years
nature-nbs-269.text: Without pest control, crop losses before harvest would typically reach 40 percent. That is why pesticides are used, but some do not go away. Persistent pesticides stay in the environment for many years. 2,4-D and atrazine can last up to 20 years, and DDT and dieldrin are also long-lived.

nature-nbs-289.title: Inga alley cropping: an alternative to slash-and-burn
nature-nbs-289.text: Slash-and-burn farming destroys forest to get a few harvests. Inga alley cropping offers another way. Crops grow between rows of nitrogen-fixing Inga trees, whose pruned leaves form a thick mulch, so land can be farmed again and again. Mike Hands developed and trialed it in Costa Rica in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

nature-nbs-287.title: Relay cropping: sowing the next crop early
nature-nbs-287.text: Relay cropping sows a second crop while the first is still growing. The first is harvested to make room for the second. A related method pairs a fast-growing crop with a slow one and harvests the fast crop first. It can out-yield either crop grown alone.

nature-nbs-264.title: Wood pasture: Europe's ancient grazing woods
nature-nbs-264.text: Since Roman times, pigs have been turned into beech and oak woods to eat acorns and beech mast. Wood pasture is a traditional European system in which open woodland gave grazing animals shelter and forage while also yielding timber and fuel. It is one of the oldest land-use practices in human history.

nature-nbs-234.title: Integrated landscape management: planning beyond the farm
nature-nbs-234.text: In 2012 Sara Scherr coined a term for planning whole regions rather than single farms or plots. Integrated landscape management brings together stakeholders who want different things from the land. By 2016 it had five steps: meet, share information, plan together, carry out the plan, then monitor and adapt. It seeks synergies among conservation, farm production and rural livelihoods.

nature-nbs-262.title: Buffers shaped by groundwater, not a ruler
nature-nbs-262.text: Groundwater enters streams at hotspots that matter greatly for temperature, acidity and nutrient retention. A hydrologically adapted buffer follows that flow, instead of a fixed width. Soil wetness maps made from elevation models show where buffers should be wider. Designing by hydrology can save money in forestry.

nature-nbs-261.title: The three zones of a riparian buffer
nature-nbs-261.text: A typical buffer runs 50 feet (15 m) on each side of a stream, in three zones. Next to the water, fast-growing native trees shade the stream and stabilize the bank. The middle zone of native shrubs gives wildlife habitat and absorbs what the outer zone misses. The outer grass zone is the first defense, slowing runoff and absorbing contaminants.

nature-nbs-244.title: Agri-environment schemes: paying farmers to farm greener
nature-nbs-244.text: In 2012 the European Commission spent €3.23 billion paying farmers to farm in greener ways. It spent only €39.6 million managing Natura 2000 sites. Agri-environment schemes are programs, compulsory for EU member states, that pay farmers to cover the cost of changing their methods. Farmers join voluntarily and commit for at least five years. In 2009 the schemes covered 38.5 million hectares, 20.9% of farmland in the then 27 EU states. Their aim has shifted, from protecting threatened habitats, to keeping wildlife on farmland, to improving services such as pollination. A 2015 review found schemes that take land out of production boosted species more than those that keep it farmed.

nature-nbs-282.title: Hedge laying: renewing an old hedge
nature-nbs-282.text: Hedge laying restores a hedge by cutting most of the way through each stem near the base, bending it over and weaving it between stakes. The partly cut stems keep living. The work encourages new growth from the base, and it was originally done to keep hedges stock-proof.

nature-nbs-281.title: Hooper's rule: dating a hedge by its species
nature-nbs-281.text: Count the woody species in a thirty-yard stretch of hedge and multiply by 110 years. That is Hooper's rule, a rule of thumb for a hedge's age. Max Hooper published it in 1974. It can be off by a couple of centuries and fails for hedges over a thousand years old.

nature-nbs-275.title: Landscape heterogeneity: variety that supports wildlife
nature-nbs-275.text: Butterflies become more abundant as a farmed landscape grows more varied. Landscape heterogeneity is that variety of habitats and features, which supports a variety of species. The Green Revolution, since 1966, spread a few crops such as wheat, rice and maize, reducing heterogeneity and local crop diversity.

nature-nbs-265.title: Regenerative economics: renewing Earth's capital
nature-nbs-265.text: Regenerative economics treats the Earth as the original capital asset, to be renewed rather than used up. In standard theory an asset can be regenerated or consumed until it yields nothing more. Supporters say ignoring nature's value has caused uneconomic growth, Herman Daly's term. The approach has four components: circulation, organizational structure, relationships and values, and collective learning. Ecological economics sets limits on the economy, while this approach focuses on renewing life in nature.

nature-nbs-266.title: Regenerative finance
nature-nbs-266.text: Regenerative finance is investing that builds on sustainable finance to support ecological health, social well-being and economic resilience. It puts the ideas of {{ref:nature-nbs-265}} into practice with money. It often, but not only, uses decentralized finance, systems that run without traditional banks.

nature-nbs-283.title: Integrated pest management: control, not eradication
nature-nbs-283.text: In 1986 Indonesia banned 57 pesticides and stopped subsidizing them. It was a bet on integrated pest management, which combines non-chemical and chemical methods to control pests economically while relying less on pesticides. The FAO describes it as mixing biological, chemical, physical and cultural methods to grow healthy crops with minimal pesticide use. Its aim is control, not eradication, since wiping out a pest is often impossible, costly and unsafe. Prevention comes first: resistant varieties, crop rotation and intercropping. Alternating between classes of control helps stop pests becoming resistant. The method runs as six repeated steps: sample, identify, learn the pest's biology, set an action threshold, choose tactics and evaluate. It reduces risks such as pest resurgence, resistance and residues on food.

nature-nbs-284.title: The economic injury level: when a pest is worth fighting
nature-nbs-284.text: A few insects in a field are not worth the cost of spraying. The economic injury level is the pest population at which crop damage would cost more than treating the pest. A lower number, the economic threshold, marks when action must be taken to keep pests from reaching that level. Integrated pest management sets these action thresholds from estimated economic damage, and treats only when they are exceeded. Thresholds depend on the pest and the site. Tolerating some pests has a hidden benefit. Letting a pest survive at a tolerable level reduces the selection pressure that breeds resistance.

nature-nbs-288.title: Push-pull cropping: repel pests here, attract them there
nature-nbs-288.text: Push-pull cropping pairs two tricks. A repellent crop pushes pests away from the main crop, while an attractive trap crop pulls them in. Trap crops alone often fail. A 2006 review of 100 trap crops found only 10 succeeded commercially, all with added measures to stop insects returning to the main crop.

reviews.working-lands: Farming carries a heavy footprint, from fertilizer runoff and plastic waste to the 13%–21% of global emissions from agriculture, forestry and land use. The practices in this chapter answer it in different ways: rotating crops, covering soil, plowing less, and weaving trees, hedges and buffers into farmland. Many save money as well as soil, yet evidence on profits and carbon is often limited or disputed, as with grazing claims and organic yields. A deeper argument runs underneath, over whether to farm intensively and spare wild land or to share farmland with wildlife. Payments such as agri-environment schemes try to make greener farming pay for the farmer.
